lesson1_1.title: What is a Robot?
lesson1_1.content:
A robot is an autonomous machine that combines sensing, decision-making, and physical action to interact with the real world. It is not just a machine that moves; it perceives its environment, adapts to new situations, and carries out tasks using its body.

On the SO-101, this means the arm can use cameras, joint encoders, and other sensors to understand where it is, then choose the correct motion and execute it smoothly.

The Sense-Think-Act Loop

Every robot operates on a fundamental loop that defines its autonomy. The loop repeats continuously so the robot can react to changing conditions.

  • Sense: The robot collects data with sensors like cameras, encoders, IMUs, or force sensors. This tells it where the arm is, where objects are, and whether the task is proceeding correctly.
  • Think: The brain of the robot processes the sensor data. It runs algorithms or AI models to estimate the best next motion, adjust for errors, and plan safe trajectories.
  • Act: The robot applies the decision using actuators such as motors, servos, and grippers. It turns electrical signals into motion to move joints.

quiz.question: Which part of the loop involves sensors like cameras collecting data?

lesson1_2.title: Degrees of Freedom (DOF)
lesson1_2.content:
Degrees of Freedom (DOF) describes how many independent motions a robot can make. Each joint gives the SO-101 one more way to position its arm.

Why 6 DOF Matters

The SO-101 has 6 DOF, which means it can place its end effector in most positions and orientations needed for manipulation. The six axes are base rotation, shoulder lift, elbow bend, wrist pitch, wrist roll, and gripper action.

quiz.question: How many independent parameters define position and orientation in 3D space?

lesson1_3.title: Coordinate Systems
lesson1_3.content:
Robots need coordinate systems to know where they are and where they should go. The two most useful systems are joint space and Cartesian space.

Joint Space

Joint space is defined by servo angles such as [q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6]. It is the natural way to command the arm's motors.

Cartesian Space

Cartesian space uses [X, Y, Z] plus orientation [Roll, Pitch, Yaw] to describe the end effector relative to the base. It is the easiest way to think about the task.

quiz.question: Which space uses X, Y, Z coordinates?

lesson2_1.title: Servo Mechanics
lesson2_1.content:
Servos are the robot’s actuators: they move joints and hold them in place. Unlike simple motors, servos are designed to reach and stay at a specified angle.

Closed-Loop Feedback

The SO-101 uses servos that report their current position back to the controller. That feedback allows the system to correct errors, improving accuracy and reliability.

quiz.question: What is a major advantage of Serial Bus Servos?

lesson2_2.title: Serial Protocol
lesson2_2.content:
The Jetson Orin Nano sends commands to the servo controller over a serial bus. Each message carries an ID, instruction code, parameters, and a checksum for safety.

Why Checksums Matter

Checksums let the controller detect interference or corrupted data. If a packet is malformed, the system ignores it instead of acting on a bad command.

quiz.question: What ensures that a serial packet wasn't corrupted?

lesson3_1.title: Forward Kinematics
lesson3_1.content:
Forward Kinematics (FK) is the mathematical process of calculating the position and orientation of the end effector, given the angles of all the joints.

Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) Parameters

In robotics, we typically use DH parameters (link lengths, twists, offsets, and angles) to systematically build transformation matrices from the base to the end effector.

lesson3_2.title: Inverse Kinematics
lesson3_2.content:
Inverse Kinematics (IK) solves the opposite problem: given a desired target position for the end effector, what joint angles are required to reach it?

Solving IK

IK can be solved analytically (using geometry) or numerically (using iterative algorithms like Jacobian-based methods). For a 6-DOF arm like the SO-101, multiple solutions may exist.

quiz.question: If a 6-DOF arm reaches a point, how many possible solutions might exist?

lesson4_1.title: Trajectory Generation
lesson4_1.content:
Trajectory generation determines the path a robot arm takes over time to get from point A to point B smoothly.

Why Smoothness Matters

Moving instantly between points causes infinite acceleration, which damages motors. We use polynomial trajectories or spline interpolation to ensure velocity and acceleration change gradually.

quiz.question: What is the primary reason for smoothing trajectories?

lesson4_2.title: Collision Avoidance
lesson4_2.content:
When planning a motion, the robot must ensure it does not collide with the environment or itself (self-collision).

Bounding Boxes

We often simplify the robot links and obstacles into geometric shapes like cylinders or bounding boxes to speed up collision detection mathematics during trajectory planning.

quiz.question: Why do we use bounding boxes for collision detection?

lesson5_1.title: Camera Calibration
lesson5_1.content:
To use vision, a robot must map pixels to the physical world. Camera calibration estimates the intrinsic parameters (focal length, distortion) and extrinsic parameters (camera's position relative to the arm).

Checkerboard Calibration

By showing a checkerboard pattern to the camera, the software can calculate a matrix that converts 2D pixel coordinates into 3D rays.

quiz.question: What pattern is commonly used to calibrate cameras?

lesson5_2.title: YOLOE Object Detection
lesson5_2.content:
YOLOE is a state-of-the-art, real-time object detection model. It allows the robot to draw bounding boxes around objects it needs to interact with.

Inference on the Edge

The SO-101 runs YOLOE locally on its Jetson Orin Nano, providing high-speed inference without relying on cloud processing, which is critical for low-latency robotics.

quiz.question: Why is running YOLOE locally important for robotics?

lesson6_1.title: Real-time Control Loops
lesson6_1.content:
A real-time control loop guarantees that code executes at a strict, deterministic interval (e.g., 100 Hz or 10ms). This ensures stable control of the robotic arm.

Jitter

If the loop timing varies (known as jitter), the arm's motion will become jerky and inaccurate. Real-time operating systems (RTOS) or high-priority threads are used to minimize jitter.

quiz.question: What happens if a control loop has high jitter?

lesson6_2.title: Final Project: Pick & Place
lesson6_2.content:
In this final challenge, you will combine Vision, Inverse Kinematics, and Trajectory Planning to perform an autonomous pick-and-place task.

The Workflow

1. Detect the object using YOLOE.
2. Calculate its 3D position using the calibrated camera.
3. Solve the IK to find joint angles.
4. Generate a smooth trajectory.
5. Execute the motion and close the gripper.

quiz.question: What is the first step in an autonomous pick-and-place task?
